Decentralized payment network and digital currency launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto. It lets people send value directly to each other without banks or any central authority, with rules enforced by thousands of independent nodes.

Smallest unit of bitcoin, equal to one hundred-millionth (0.00000001) of a coin, named after Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous author of the Bitcoin whitepaper. Small payments and Lightning amounts are usually expressed in this unit.

Informal plural of satoshi, the smallest unit of bitcoin. Many bitcoiners count balances and prices in sats, and saving small amounts regularly is often described as stacking sats. Lightning payments are typically denominated in them.

Surname used by the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, who published the whitepaper in 2008 and the first software in 2009, then stepped away in 2010 or 2011. The real identity behind the name has never been confirmed.

Bundle of transactions added to the Bitcoin ledger about every ten minutes. Each block includes the hash of the previous one, linking them in order, and its limited size means transactions compete through fees to be included.

Sequence of blocks linked by including each previous block's hash. Nodes follow the valid chain with the most accumulated proof of work, and altering any past block would invalidate every block built after it.

Append-only ledger made of blocks linked by cryptographic hashes, recording every Bitcoin transaction since 2009. Copies are kept by many independent nodes, making the history public and extremely hard to rewrite.

Participant who spends electricity and specialized hardware searching for a valid proof of work to add the next block. In return, the miner collects the block subsidy plus the fees of the transactions it chose to include.

Process of competing to add new blocks by performing proof of work. It secures the network by making attacks costly, orders transactions, and is the only way new bitcoins are issued, through the block subsidy.

Computer running Bitcoin software that downloads and independently checks every block and transaction against the consensus rules, rejecting invalid ones. Running your own node lets you verify payments without trusting third parties.

Scheduled event every 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years, that cuts the new-coin subsidy paid to miners in half. It enforces Bitcoin's predictable, decreasing issuance; the 2024 halving reduced it to 3.125 BTC per block.

Fixed-length output of a cryptographic function that acts as a unique fingerprint of any data; any tiny change produces a completely different result. Bitcoin uses SHA-256 hashes to link blocks, identify transactions and do proof of work.

Number used once: a 32-bit field in the block header that miners change repeatedly, hashing the header each time, until they find a hash below the difficulty target. It is the core variable of proof-of-work mining.

Software or device that generates and stores the private keys needed to receive and spend bitcoin. Coins stay on the blockchain; the wallet holds the keys. Hot wallets are connected to the internet, cold wallets are kept offline.

Backup of a wallet, usually a list of 12 or 24 words under the BIP39 standard, from which all its keys can be regenerated. Whoever has it controls the funds, so it must be stored safely offline; losing it can mean losing the coins.

Cryptographic number used to control bitcoin. The private key signs transactions and must stay secret; the public key, derived from it, is used to create addresses and verify signatures. Hence the saying: not your keys, not your coins.

Cryptographic proof, created with a private key, that the owner authorized a transaction. Anyone can check it against the public key without learning the private key. Bitcoin uses ECDSA and, since Taproot, Schnorr signatures.

Set of valid but unconfirmed transactions that each node keeps while they wait to be included in a block. When it grows crowded, users bid higher fees, and miners usually pick the transactions that pay the most per byte.

Second-layer network built on top of Bitcoin that enables near-instant, low-fee payments through a web of payment channels. Most payments happen off-chain, with the base blockchain used only to open and close channels.

Two-party arrangement on Lightning, opened and closed with on-chain transactions, that lets both sides exchange payments off-chain by updating a shared balance. Many linked channels let payments route across the whole network.

Soft-fork upgrade activated in 2021 that introduced Schnorr signatures and new script structures. It makes complex spending conditions look like ordinary payments when used cooperatively, improving privacy, efficiency and flexibility.

Segregated Witness: soft fork activated in 2017 that moved signature data into a separate structure. It fixed transaction malleability, effectively raised block capacity and made second layers such as Lightning practical.

Digital signature scheme devised by German cryptographer Claus Schnorr and added to Bitcoin with Taproot. Its signatures are compact, simple to verify, and can be combined so that multiple signers produce a single signature.

Refers to Ralph Merkle, a pioneer of public-key cryptography, and to the Merkle tree he invented: a structure that hashes data in pairs up to a single root. Bitcoin blocks commit to their transactions with it, allowing compact inclusion proofs.

Name of the first Bitcoin block, mined by Satoshi Nakamoto on January 3, 2009. It is the only block without a predecessor, and its coinbase contains a newspaper headline about bank bailouts, a timestamp and a statement of purpose.

Measure of how hard it is to find a valid proof of work. It readjusts every 2016 blocks, rising when more hashpower joins and falling when it leaves, to keep the average time between blocks close to ten minutes.

Newly created bitcoins a miner receives for each valid block, in addition to transaction fees. It started at 50 BTC and halves every 210,000 blocks, which is how all new bitcoins enter circulation until issuance ends.

Amount a sender pays to have a transaction included in a block, collected by the miner. It depends on the transaction's size in virtual bytes and on demand for block space, not on the amount sent, and is usually quoted in sats per vbyte.

Unspent Transaction Output: an amount of bitcoin locked to spending conditions and not yet spent. Bitcoin tracks these pieces instead of account balances; wallets combine UTXOs as inputs to make payments and return change as a new one.
Transaction ID: the hash that uniquely identifies a Bitcoin transaction. Entering it into a block explorer shows whether a payment has been confirmed, in which block, and with how many confirmations.

Condition of being limited in supply. Bitcoin's scarcity is enforced by code: there will never be more than 21 million coins, and nobody can create extra ones, a key reason it is compared to gold as a store of value.

Agreement among independent nodes on which transactions and blocks are valid, achieved because each one enforces the same rules. If groups of nodes enforce incompatible rules, consensus breaks and the chain can split.

Backward-compatible change to Bitcoin's rules that tightens what is valid, so nodes that don't upgrade still accept the new blocks. SegWit and Taproot were activated this way, which is the preferred method for upgrades.
Change to the consensus rules that loosens or alters them so that non-upgraded nodes reject the new blocks, splitting the chain if not everyone follows. Bitcoin Cash was created this way in 2017.

Science of protecting information with mathematics, from the Greek for hidden writing. Bitcoin relies on it for hash functions, which link blocks and power mining, and for digital signatures, which prove ownership of coins.

Ability to choose what personal or financial information to reveal and to whom. Bitcoin's ledger is public, so users protect it with practices such as fresh addresses, CoinJoin and Lightning. Cypherpunks see it as essential to a free society.

Activist who promotes privacy and individual freedom through strong cryptography and working code. The cypherpunk mailing lists and community of the 1990s laid the ideas and tools from which Bitcoin later emerged.

Nine-page document 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System', published by Satoshi Nakamoto on October 31, 2008 on a cryptography mailing list. It describes how proof of work and a chain of blocks solve double spending without a trusted party.
Slang for holding bitcoin long term instead of selling during price swings. It began as a misspelling of 'hold' in a 2013 forum post and is often reinterpreted as the backronym Hold On for Dear Life.

Control and safekeeping of the private keys that move bitcoin. With third-party custody, such as an exchange, the provider holds the keys; with self-custody, the owner holds them and alone bears responsibility for their security.

Setup that requires several signatures from different keys to spend funds, such as 2-of-3. It removes single points of failure and is used by companies, families and inheritance plans to protect bitcoin against loss or theft.

Family of protocols based on Schnorr signatures that let several parties jointly produce one aggregated signature for one combined key. A multisig spend then looks like a single-signer payment, saving space and improving privacy.

Extended public key: a key from which a wallet can derive all its receiving addresses without being able to spend. It is shared with watch-only wallets or services to track balances, though it reveals the wallet's full history.

Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction: standard format, defined in BIP174, for passing an unsigned or partly signed transaction between wallets and devices. It makes multisig and hardware-wallet signing interoperable.

String, derived from a public key or script, that someone shares to receive bitcoin. Modern formats start with bc1. Using a new address for each payment is recommended to protect privacy, and wallets generate them automatically.

Separate Bitcoin network where coins have no monetary value, used by developers and learners to test software and practice without risking real funds. Test coins are usually obtained for free from websites called faucets.

Application-Specific Integrated Circuit: a chip designed for a single task. Bitcoin ASICs compute SHA-256 hashes far more efficiently than CPUs or graphics cards, which they replaced, and they now dominate mining.

Group of miners who combine their hashpower and share block rewards in proportion to the work each contributes. Pools give small miners steadier, more predictable income instead of rare, irregular wins.

Each block added on top of the block containing a transaction. More confirmations make reversal increasingly unlikely; six is a common threshold for large amounts, while zero means the transaction is still in the mempool.

Physical resource that proof of work converts into security: attacking Bitcoin would require spending comparable real energy. Miners seek the cheapest power, often surplus or stranded sources that would otherwise go unused.

Sustained rise in general prices, often driven by expanding money supply, which erodes the purchasing power of fiat currency. Bitcoin's fixed and predictable issuance, capped at 21 million coins, is designed to resist it.

Government-issued money whose value rests on legal decree rather than on a commodity, such as the peso, dollar or euro. Its supply can be expanded at will by central banks, the main contrast drawn with Bitcoin's fixed supply.

Precious metal used as money for millennia because it is scarce, durable and costly to extract. Bitcoin is often called digital gold because it shares those traits while being easier to divide, verify and transport.
Anything widely accepted as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. Bitcoin aims to be sound money: scarce, verifiable and independent of any state or central bank.

Self-determination and independence. Financial sovereignty means controlling your own money without depending on intermediaries that can freeze or censor it; with Bitcoin, holding your own keys makes you, in effect, your own bank.

Hal Finney, cryptographer and early cypherpunk who ran Bitcoin from its first days, received the first Bitcoin transaction from Satoshi Nakamoto in January 2009 and helped test and improve the early software.

Nick Szabo, computer scientist and legal scholar who coined the term smart contract and designed Bit Gold, a proposal for scarce digital money based on proof of work, widely regarded as a direct precursor of Bitcoin.

Proof-of-work system proposed by Adam Back in 1997 to fight email spam by making each message require a small computational effort. The Bitcoin whitepaper cites it, and mining uses the same basic idea.
Design for decentralized digital money proposed by Nick Szabo, combining proof of work, timestamping and unforgeable scarcity. It was never implemented, but many of its ideas anticipated Bitcoin.
Food at the center of the first well-known real-world purchase with bitcoin: on May 22, 2010, two pizzas were bought for 10,000 BTC. The date is celebrated every year as Bitcoin Pizza Day.

Laszlo Hanyecz, programmer who made the famous May 2010 purchase of two pizzas for 10,000 BTC, celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day. He is also credited as an early pioneer of mining bitcoin with graphics cards (GPUs).

Open, decentralized protocol for publishing signed notes through independent relays, used mainly for social networking. Identities are cryptographic keys, so no company owns accounts; it is popular among bitcoiners and integrates Lightning payments.
Small Lightning payment sent to a post or user, especially on Nostr, as a tip or a form of appreciation. It works like a like that carries real value, typically a few sats delivered instantly.

Privacy technique in which several users combine their inputs and outputs into one collaborative transaction, making it hard to link who paid whom. Participants keep control of their coins throughout; no one takes custody.

Transaction in which both the payer and the receiver contribute inputs. It breaks the common assumption that all inputs belong to one owner, improving privacy for everyone, and looks like an ordinary payment on-chain.

Bitcoin's simple, stack-based programming language used to define the conditions for spending an output, such as requiring a valid signature. It is deliberately limited, without loops, to keep validation safe and predictable.

Condition that prevents bitcoin from being spent until a certain time or block height has passed. It is used in payment channels, vaults and inheritance setups, and is enforced by the consensus rules through script.

Business where users buy and sell bitcoin, usually against fiat currencies. Convenient for acquiring coins, but funds left there are held by the exchange, so users depend on its solvency and honesty until they withdraw.

Know Your Customer: identity checks, such as ID documents and selfies, that regulated exchanges and financial services require from users. It links a person's identity to their purchases, with implications for privacy.

Optional extra word or phrase added to a seed under BIP39, sometimes called the 25th word. Each passphrase opens a different wallet, adding protection if the seed is found, but forgetting it makes the funds unrecoverable.

Service that monitors Lightning channels on a user's behalf while their node is offline. If a counterparty tries to close a channel with an outdated state, it broadcasts the penalty transaction that protects the user's funds.

Quick Response code: a square black-and-white pattern that encodes data readable by a camera. Wallets use it to share addresses and Lightning invoices, so payments can be made by scanning instead of typing long strings.

Separate blockchain with its own rules, to which bitcoin can be moved through a two-way peg and later moved back. It allows experimenting with features not available on Bitcoin; Liquid and Rootstock are examples.

Federated sidechain developed by Blockstream, where a group of members secures the peg and produces one-minute blocks. It offers faster settlement and confidential transactions using L-BTC, a token backed by bitcoin.

Protocol created by Casey Rodarmor that assigns a number to every satoshi so individual sats can be tracked, and that allows inscribing data such as images onto them. It started a debate about using block space for non-monetary data.

Proof that a piece of data existed at a given time. The whitepaper describes Bitcoin as a distributed timestamp server: each block fixes the order of transactions in time, and data can be anchored in the chain for proof of existence.
Record of accounts listing transactions and balances. Bitcoin's blockchain is a public ledger that anyone can download and audit. The word is also the name of a well-known hardware wallet brand.

Reliance on others to behave honestly. Bitcoin replaces trust in banks and intermediaries with verification by each node; the whitepaper criticizes electronic payments that depend on trusted third parties.
To check something yourself instead of relying on others. Every node verifies each new block and transaction against the rules, which gives rise to the Bitcoin motto: don't trust, verify.

Process by which new bitcoins are created, through the block subsidy paid to miners. It follows a fixed, public schedule that halves roughly every four years and approaches the 21 million cap, ending around the year 2140.
A thousand thousand. In Bitcoin it refers to the hard supply cap of 21 million coins set by the protocol, a limit that every node enforces and that underpins bitcoin's scarcity.

Financial institutions that take deposits and lend money. The genesis block quotes a headline about a second government bailout for banks, and Bitcoin was created as an alternative that does not depend on them.

The Times, a British newspaper whose January 3, 2009 headline, 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks', Satoshi embedded in the genesis block as a timestamp and a comment on the financial system.

Title of the UK finance minister, the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The office is named in the headline embedded in Bitcoin's genesis block, which reported he was on the brink of a second bailout for banks.

Rescue of a failing company, especially a bank, with public money. Bank bailouts after the 2008 financial crisis are referenced in the genesis block and are often cited as part of the motivation for Bitcoin.

Money in physical form that passes directly from hand to hand without intermediaries. The Bitcoin whitepaper's title describes a peer-to-peer electronic cash system: digital money with the same direct quality.
Relating to digital devices and data rather than paper. The whitepaper title, 'A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System', describes Bitcoin as cash that exists and moves entirely in electronic form.

An equal participant. In a peer-to-peer network, like the one named in the whitepaper title, nodes connect directly to each other with no central server, and each node is a peer that relays blocks and transactions.
Bitcoin Improvement Proposal: the standard document format used to propose and describe changes to Bitcoin or related conventions. For example, BIP39 defines seed words and BIP141 describes SegWit.
Units that make up a seed phrase. Under BIP39, a wallet backup consists of 12 or 24 words chosen from an official list of 2048, written on paper or stamped on steel so the wallet can be restored.

Describes keys that are kept fully offline, as in cold storage or a cold wallet. Keeping private keys away from internet-connected devices greatly reduces the risk of remote theft; the opposite is a hot wallet.

Physical equipment, as opposed to software. A hardware wallet is a dedicated device that generates and stores private keys offline and signs transactions internally, so the keys never touch an internet-connected computer.
To accumulate bitcoin gradually, usually by buying small amounts regularly, as in stacking sats. The word also names the total amount someone has saved in bitcoin.

Dollar-Cost Averaging: strategy of buying a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price. It smooths out volatility and removes the need to time the market, and is a common way to accumulate bitcoin.
All-Time High: the highest price an asset has ever reached. Bitcoin markets frequently mark a new one after long cycles, and the term is widely used in price discussions.

Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt: misleading or exaggerated negative claims spread to scare people away from something. In Bitcoin, it describes recurring rumors and alarmist stories about bans, energy or security.
Short for plebeians: term ordinary bitcoiners use proudly for themselves. It refers to everyday users, not large holders or celebrities, who often run their own nodes and hold their own keys.
Modest and free of arrogance. The popular saying 'stay humble, stack sats' urges bitcoiners to avoid boasting when prices rise and to keep saving steadily regardless of market moves.

Degree to which someone favors something. Time preference measures how much a person values the present over the future; low time preference means saving and planning long term, which bitcoiners link to sound money.
Short click of a clock. In Bitcoin culture, the phrase tick tock, next block evokes the steady rhythm of new blocks arriving about every ten minutes, regardless of what happens in the world.
Short for Bitcoin maximalist: a person who considers Bitcoin the only cryptocurrency worth using or holding and views alternative coins as unnecessary or harmful distractions.
Any cryptocurrency other than bitcoin, short for alternative coin. Many began as copies or variations of Bitcoin's code; critics, including maximalists, often dismiss them more harshly as shitcoins.

OP_RETURN: script opcode that marks a transaction output as provably unspendable and lets it carry a small amount of arbitrary data. It is used to embed messages and commitments in the chain without bloating the UTXO set.

Latin American Bitcoin and Blockchain Conference: an annual event born in Buenos Aires in 2013 and held in different cities across the region. It is one of the longest-running Bitcoin conferences in the world.
Total amount of a currency in existence. Bitcoin's supply is fixed by protocol at a maximum of 21 million coins and follows a predetermined schedule, so it does not grow when demand rises.

Degree to which a price moves up and down over time. Bitcoin's price has historically swung sharply, which can unsettle short-term holders; its volatility has tended to decline as the market has grown.
Capable of being split into smaller parts. Bitcoin can be divided to eight decimal places, down to one satoshi, so it can be used for both large transfers and small everyday payments.

Interchangeable: each unit is equivalent to any other of the same kind. Money needs this property, but because Bitcoin's history is public, coins can be traced or labeled as tainted, which challenges it.
Possible to inspect and check independently. Anyone running a node can verify Bitcoin's full transaction history and total supply, without relying on official reports or trusted auditors.

Blocking or suppressing communication or payments by an authority. Bitcoin is designed for censorship resistance: no bank, company or government can stop a valid transaction from being broadcast and eventually included in a block.

Authorization from someone else to act. Bitcoin is permissionless: anyone can run a node, create a wallet, mine or send a payment without asking a bank, company or government for approval or identifying themselves.

Frontiers between countries, often controlled for money moving across them. Bitcoin ignores them: a payment to another country works like a local one, and a person can carry access to their funds simply by memorizing a seed phrase.

Exaggerated excitement around an asset, often amplified by social media and promotion. In crypto markets, hype tends to drive sharp price rises followed by crashes; many bitcoiners favor long-term fundamentals over short-lived euphoria.

Relating to quantum mechanics. Quantum computers use qubits and, if built at large enough scale, could break the elliptic curve signatures Bitcoin uses today. The threat is still theoretical, and post-quantum signature schemes are being studied.

Set of rules that defines how computers communicate and what counts as valid. Bitcoin is an open protocol, not a company: every node independently enforces the same consensus rules about blocks, transactions and the coin supply.

Instructions written by programmers that computers execute. Bitcoin's software is open source, so anyone can read, audit and propose changes to it; this transparency lets users verify the rules instead of trusting an authority.

System of interconnected computers that exchange information. Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer network of thousands of nodes relaying transactions and blocks with no central server; Lightning is a payment network built on top of it.

Signed message that moves bitcoin by spending existing outputs (inputs) and creating new ones (outputs). The difference between them is the fee paid to miners. It is broadcast to the network and becomes final once included in a block.

Part of a transaction that references and spends a previous unspent output. Each input must provide valid proof, usually a signature, that its owner authorized the spend. The sum of the inputs funds the outputs plus the fee.

Part of a transaction that assigns an amount of bitcoin to a locking condition, such as an address. While unspent it is called a UTXO and can later be used as an input; each output can be spent only once.

Amount returned to the sender when the inputs of a transaction are worth more than the payment. Because outputs must be spent whole, wallets create a change output back to the user; handling it carefully helps preserve privacy.

Total amount of funds available in an account or wallet. In Bitcoin there are no account balances on the chain: a wallet calculates its balance by adding up the unspent outputs (UTXOs) its keys can spend.

Transfer of money to settle a purchase or debt. In Bitcoin it can be made on-chain, final after confirmations, or over Lightning, where it arrives in seconds for very low fees, often by scanning a QR code.

Request for payment. On Lightning, an invoice is an encoded string, usually starting with lnbc on mainnet, that contains the amount, a description, an expiry time and the payment hash; the payer scans or pastes it to pay.

Path a payment follows. On Lightning, the sender's node searches for a sequence of channels with enough liquidity to reach the recipient; if no suitable route exists, the payment fails and must be retried another way.

Ease with which funds can move or be traded. On Lightning, it is the balance available on each side of a channel: outbound liquidity lets you send and inbound liquidity lets you receive. In markets, it means trading without moving the price.

Level of a system built on top of another. Bitcoin is the base layer, which prioritizes security and decentralization; second layers such as Lightning add speed and lower costs while settling back to the base chain.

Open-source protocol for federated ecash on Bitcoin. A group of guardians jointly holds the bitcoin in multisig and issues private ecash tokens, aiming to give communities custody that is shared and more private than a single custodian.

Electronic cash based on David Chaum's blind signatures, which let a mint issue tokens it cannot link to the user who redeems them. Modern ecash systems such as Cashu and Fedimint back tokens with bitcoin, offering strong payment privacy.

Open-source ecash protocol for Bitcoin in which a single mint holds bitcoin and issues blinded tokens. Tokens can be sent as plain text strings and work with Lightning; users trust the mint for custody but gain strong privacy.

Spare copy of important data kept in case the original is lost. In Bitcoin, the key backup is the seed phrase written down on paper or metal; without it, losing or breaking a wallet device can mean losing the funds forever.
Strong iron alloy resistant to fire, water and corrosion. Bitcoiners stamp or engrave their seed words on steel plates or capsules so the backup survives disasters that would destroy paper.

Measure of randomness or unpredictability. A wallet's security depends on generating its seed from high entropy; if the randomness is weak or predictable, an attacker could guess the private keys and take the funds.

Small cubes with numbered faces used to generate random numbers. Some bitcoiners roll dice to create their own seed entropy, avoiding reliance on a device's random number generator; around 99 rolls of a six-sided die give 256 bits.

Small value computed from data to detect errors. In a BIP39 seed, the last word contains a checksum, and Bitcoin addresses include one too, so a typo is usually caught instead of sending funds to a wrong address.

Process of generating keys from a single seed in a hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallet. A derivation path such as m/84'/0'/0' tells the wallet which branch of keys to use, so the same seed restores the same addresses.
Open to everyone. A public key is derived from a private key and can be shared safely; addresses are derived from it, and others use it to verify signatures without ever learning the private key.

Restricted to its owner. A private key is a secret number that controls bitcoin by producing signatures; anyone who obtains it can spend the funds, so it must never be shared and is usually derived from a backed-up seed.

Line that bends rather than staying straight. Bitcoin uses the elliptic curve secp256k1: mathematics on this curve lets a public key be derived from a private key easily but makes reversing the process infeasible.

Source that provides external information, such as a price or the result of an event, to a contract or protocol. In Bitcoin, oracles can sign outcomes so that smart contracts like discreet log contracts settle without trusting a middleman.

Secure place for storing valuables. In Bitcoin, a vault is a custody setup that delays withdrawals so the owner can cancel a theft in time; proposals such as OP_VAULT would make this protection easier to build.

Binding agreement or promise. In Bitcoin, a covenant is a proposed mechanism that restricts where coins can be sent in future transactions. Proposals such as CTV and OP_VAULT are debated for uses like vaults and scaling.

Short for chain reorganization: when nodes switch to a competing branch with more accumulated work, recent blocks are discarded and their transactions return to the mempool. Waiting for several confirmations protects against it.

Something left without its parents. In Bitcoin, an orphan or stale block is a valid block that ends up outside the main chain, typically when two miners find blocks at almost the same time and the other branch wins.

Opening section of a document or data structure. A Bitcoin block header is 80 bytes holding the version, previous block hash, Merkle root, timestamp, difficulty target and nonce; miners hash it repeatedly to find a valid block.

Vertical measure of something. A block's height is its position in the chain counted from the genesis block, which has height zero. Events like halvings are scheduled by height, for example block 840,000 for the fourth halving.
Distinct period of time. In Bitcoin, an epoch is the span of 2016 blocks, about two weeks, after which the mining difficulty is recalculated; there are also halving epochs of 210,000 blocks.

Change made to correct or adapt something. Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment recalculates every 2016 blocks how hard mining is, based on how long the last period took, keeping the average time between blocks near ten minutes.

Total computing power devoted to mining, measured in hashes per second, today in exahashes. A higher hashrate makes the network more expensive to attack, since an attacker would need to match a large share of it.

First transaction in each block, created by the miner to collect the block subsidy plus fees; it has no inputs from previous outputs. The genesis block's coinbase field contained a newspaper headline. It is also the name of a large exchange.

Central or essential part of something. Bitcoin Core is the reference and most widely used full node software, descended from Satoshi's original client and maintained as open source by many contributors.

Fastenings tied in rope, or a unit of speed at sea. Bitcoin Knots is a full node implementation derived from Bitcoin Core and maintained by Luke Dashjr, offering extra options, including stricter mempool policies.

Invented name used instead of a real one. Satoshi Nakamoto is the pseudonym of Bitcoin's creator. Bitcoin itself is pseudonymous: addresses are not names, but all transactions are public and can be analyzed and linked.

State of being unidentified. Bitcoin does not guarantee it: every transaction is permanently public, and addresses can be linked to people through analysis or exchange KYC records, so privacy requires careful practices.

Close monitoring of people's activity, often by governments or corporations. Financial surveillance tracks how people earn and spend; privacy tools in Bitcoin aim to limit it, while central bank digital currencies could expand it.

Central Bank Digital Currency: digital form of a national currency issued directly by a central bank, such as China's digital yuan. Critics warn it allows monitoring and programmable control of payments, unlike Bitcoin.

Reduction in a currency's value relative to other currencies or goods. Repeated devaluations, as experienced in Argentina, erode savings and push people toward assets outside the issuer's control, such as dollars or bitcoin.

Currency of the United States and the world's main reserve currency. Many Argentines save in dollars to escape inflation, using the informal 'blue' exchange rate, and bitcoin's price is most often quoted in dollars.

Money set aside for future use. Inflation erodes savings held in fiat currency; many bitcoiners see bitcoin, with its fixed supply, as a long-term savings tool, despite its short-term price volatility.

Money sent by a migrant worker to family in their home country. Traditional remittance services can charge high fees and take days; bitcoin, especially over Lightning, can deliver such transfers quickly and for very little.
Process of beginning to use something. Bitcoin adoption measures how many people, businesses and countries use it; El Salvador making bitcoin legal tender in 2021 was a widely noted milestone.

Buying and selling of goods and services. Bitcoin commerce includes shops and online stores accepting bitcoin, increasingly through Lightning, which allows instant, low-fee payments at the point of sale.
Place or system where buyers and sellers trade and prices are set. Bitcoin's price is formed on many exchanges worldwide; markets alternate between rising bull phases and falling bear phases.
Investor who expects prices to rise, symbolized by a bull thrusting its horns upward. A bull market or bull run is a prolonged period of rising prices, which Bitcoin has gone through several times.

Investor who expects prices to fall, symbolized by a bear swiping its paws downward. A bear market is a prolonged decline; in Bitcoin these periods have often lasted many months and are sometimes called crypto winters.
Large sea mammal, and slang for a person or entity holding a very large amount of an asset. Bitcoin whales can move the market with big trades, so their on-chain movements are closely watched.
Earth's natural satellite. In crypto slang, 'to the moon' expresses the hope that a price will rise dramatically; the expression became a meme during Bitcoin's bull runs.

Token designed to keep a stable value by tracking a reference asset, usually the US dollar. Examples include USDT and USDC; they are issued by companies holding reserves and can be frozen, unlike bitcoin.

Person or institution that holds and safeguards assets on behalf of others. Exchanges and custodial wallets hold users' private keys, so users depend on their honesty and security; hence the saying not your keys, not your coins.

Holding your own private keys rather than leaving bitcoin with a third party. Self-custody makes you your own bank: no one can freeze or lose your funds, but you are responsible for securing and backing up your seed.

Very small payment, sometimes worth a few satoshis. Lightning makes micropayments practical thanks to tiny fees, enabling models such as paying per article, per minute of streaming or per API call instead of subscribing.

Informal in-person gathering of people with a shared interest. Bitcoin meetups bring together local users and developers to learn, exchange experience and often make their first payments, and exist in cities worldwide.

Group of people who share interests or values. Bitcoin's global community of users, developers, educators and miners has no leader; it sustains the project through volunteering, open debate and local groups such as Argentina's.

Ability of the mind to store and recall information. Memorizing a seed phrase, sometimes called a brain wallet, lets someone carry access to bitcoin without physical backups, though forgetting it means losing the funds.

Assets passed on to heirs after someone dies. With bitcoin, heirs need access to the keys, so planning matters; tools such as multisig, timelocks and clear instructions help pass on funds without exposing them during life.

Capacity to recover from shocks and keep functioning. Bitcoin's resilience comes from its distributed nodes and miners: it has continued operating through exchange collapses, price crashes and government bans.

Unable to be changed. Once a transaction is buried under enough blocks, rewriting it would require redoing an enormous amount of proof of work, so Bitcoin's transaction history is considered practically immutable.
Not taking any side. Bitcoin is called neutral money because its rules apply equally to everyone: it does not check who is paying, for what purpose or from which country.
Instrument for measuring time. Bitcoin works as a decentralized clock: each new block, roughly every ten minutes, is a tick that orders transactions in time without a central timekeeper.

Person who travels into unknown places. A block explorer is a website, such as mempool.space, that shows blocks, transactions, addresses and fees on the blockchain; running your own instance improves privacy.

Fine particles of dirt. In Bitcoin, dust refers to outputs so small that the fee required to spend them would cost more than they are worth; dust is sometimes sent to addresses to try to track their owners.

To combine several things into one. In Bitcoin, consolidation merges many small UTXOs into a single output in one transaction, ideally when fees are low, so future spending is cheaper, though it can link addresses together.

Tag that identifies or describes something. Wallets let users label addresses, transactions and UTXOs with notes about their origin; this helps with accounting and with coin control to avoid mixing coins and hurting privacy.

Bitcoin test network where blocks must be signed by designated signers in addition to the normal rules. It is more stable and predictable than testnet, letting developers test software with coins that have no value.

The Onion Router: free network that hides a user's IP address by routing traffic through several encrypted relays. Many Bitcoin and Lightning nodes run over Tor to protect their location and owners' privacy.

Software permanently stored in a hardware device that controls how it works. A hardware wallet's firmware generates keys and signs transactions, so users should install updates only from verified official sources.

Adi Shamir, Israeli cryptographer and the S in the RSA algorithm. His secret sharing scheme splits a secret into parts so that only a set number of them can rebuild it, an idea used for some seed backup methods.

Exchange of one thing for another. In Bitcoin, swaps move value between networks or assets, such as Lightning and on-chain; an atomic swap either completes fully on both sides or does not happen at all, removing counterparty risk.
Vessel that travels underwater. A submarine swap exchanges on-chain bitcoin for Lightning funds or the reverse, using the same hash lock on both sides so that neither party can cheat the other.

Value that produces a given output when passed through a hash function. In Lightning, the recipient keeps a secret preimage whose hash locks the payment; revealing it along the route completes the payment and proves it was made.

Bulb vegetable made of layers. Onion routing wraps a message in several layers of encryption so each relay only learns the previous and next hop; Lightning payments and the Tor network both use this design for privacy.

Something kept back for future use. Central banks hold reserves of gold and foreign currency; some governments and companies have considered or adopted bitcoin as a reserve asset meant to be held long term.

Use of borrowed money to enlarge an investment position. Leverage multiplies both gains and losses; in volatile bitcoin markets, leveraged traders are frequently liquidated when prices move against them.
To use money to pay for something. In Bitcoin, spending consumes outputs, each of which can be spent only once; Bitcoin solved the double-spend problem of digital money without a central authority.

To transmit to many recipients at once. After a transaction is signed, a wallet broadcasts it to nodes, which check it and relay it to their peers until it reaches miners and can be included in a block.

Term many bitcoiners prefer for the blockchain, inspired by Satoshi's early code, which described the chain as a sequence of timestamped blocks. It emphasizes Bitcoin's role in ordering events in time.
Spread across many places or participants. Bitcoin's ledger is distributed among thousands of independent nodes, each with a full copy, so there is no single point of failure or control.
Ability to wait calmly. Long-term bitcoin holders need patience to endure bear markets and volatility; it is linked to low time preference, the idea of valuing the future over immediate consumption.

Person who uses, studies, promotes or builds on Bitcoin. The term covers ordinary users, often calling themselves plebs, as well as developers, miners and educators who share an interest in sound, open money.

Adam Back, British cryptographer who created Hashcash in 1997, a proof-of-work system cited in the Bitcoin whitepaper and an inspiration for Bitcoin mining. He later co-founded and leads the company Blockstream.

Andreas Antonopoulos, Bitcoin educator and author of Mastering Bitcoin, a widely used technical book. His talks, collected in The Internet of Money, introduced many people to Bitcoin's technology and significance.
Wei Dai, computer engineer and cypherpunk who in 1998 proposed b-money, a design for anonymous distributed electronic cash. It is cited in the Bitcoin whitepaper as one of its precursors.

Eric Hughes, mathematician and cypherpunk who wrote A Cypherpunk's Manifesto in 1993, arguing that privacy is necessary for an open society. He co-founded the cypherpunks mailing list, where digital cash ideas were discussed.
Tim May, engineer and writer who co-founded the cypherpunk movement and wrote The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto, predicting that cryptography would let people interact and trade beyond state control.

David Chaum, cryptographer who invented blind signatures in the early 1980s and founded DigiCash, an early electronic cash company. His work is the basis of modern ecash systems such as Cashu and Fedimint.

Gavin Andresen, software developer to whom Satoshi Nakamoto handed leadership of the Bitcoin project in 2010. He created an early faucet that gave away free bitcoins to attract users and helped found the Bitcoin Foundation.

Gregory Maxwell, cryptographer and longtime Bitcoin Core developer. He proposed CoinJoin to improve transaction privacy, designed confidential transactions to hide amounts, and co-founded the company Blockstream.

Pieter Wuille, Bitcoin Core developer who co-authored Segregated Witness and Taproot, which brought Schnorr signatures to Bitcoin. He also co-designed the bech32 address format and led work on the libsecp256k1 library.

Joseph Poon, co-author with Thaddeus Dryja of the paper that proposed the Lightning Network, a system of payment channels for fast, cheap Bitcoin payments. He later co-proposed Plasma, a scaling design for Ethereum.

Thaddeus Dryja, co-author with Joseph Poon of the Lightning Network paper. As a researcher at MIT's Digital Currency Initiative, he created Utreexo, a design to drastically reduce the storage needed by full nodes.

Michael Saylor, executive who turned his software company MicroStrategy, later renamed Strategy, into the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, a strategy copied by other public companies. He is a prominent Bitcoin advocate.

Saifedean Ammous, economist influenced by the Austrian school and author of The Bitcoin Standard, a bestselling book presenting bitcoin as sound money. He followed it with The Fiat Standard, a critique of government money.

Jack Dorsey, co-founder of Twitter and founder of Square, renamed Block, which builds Bitcoin products. A strong Bitcoin supporter, he has funded open-source development, including the decentralized social protocol Nostr.

Jameson Lopp, software engineer and co-founder of Casa, a company offering multisig custody. He is a well-known voice on Bitcoin security, privacy and self-custody, and maintains a public list of physical attacks on bitcoin holders.

Jack Mallers, founder and CEO of Strike, a Lightning-based payments app. In 2021 he emotionally announced at a Bitcoin conference that El Salvador would make bitcoin legal tender, with Strike's involvement.

Alex Gladstein, chief strategy officer at the Human Rights Foundation, which organizes the Oslo Freedom Forum. He writes and speaks about Bitcoin as a tool for people living under authoritarian regimes and inflation.

Hal Finney, cryptographer and cypherpunk who created reusable proof of work (RPOW). He was the first person to run Bitcoin after Satoshi, tweeting 'Running bitcoin', and received the first bitcoin transaction in January 2009.

Ralph Merkle, computer scientist and a pioneer of public-key cryptography. He invented Merkle trees, hash structures that Bitcoin uses to summarize all transactions in a block into a single root stored in its header.
